builder_plan.scenario: A self-hosted assistant is too expensive because its model uses most of the GPU memory.
builder_plan.change: Try the paper's supported lower-precision weights on a copy of your serving setup.
builder_plan.baseline: The same model at its original precision, on the same GPU.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Peak memory, task pass rate, latency, and total serving cost at the same context and load.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: BQ-LoRA: Binary-Quantized Low-Rank Adapters as Implicit Regularizers for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
summary: BQ-LoRA replaces the FP16 low-rank adapters used in QLoRA with 1-bit binarized adapters plus a learned per-layer scale and a Scaled Straight-Through Estimator, while keeping the 4-bit quantized base model unchanged. Training memory matches QLoRA and step time rises by under 4%, so the cost is implementation complexity and, for serving gains, dependence on a prototype extension of Punica's SGMV kernel; storage savings apply at inference and adapter-serving time only. The advantage is not uniform: on LLaMA-2 it loses to LoftQ at 7B and QLoRA at 70B, binarization with STE can be sensitive to scale and threshold initialization, and results rest on a single paper whose deployment kernel is a research prototype without production hardening.
rationale: The method directly reduces adapter storage and serving memory on hardware the reader already has, but the quality advantage is model-family-dependent and the serving gains require a research-grade custom kernel, so small-scale validation on the reader's specific models is warranted before adoption.

claims.statement: BQ-LoRA replaces the FP16 low-rank adapters used in QLoRA with 1-bit binarized adapters plus a learned per-layer scale and a Scaled Straight-Through Estimator, while keeping the 4-bit quantized base model unchanged. Training memory matches QLoRA and step time rises by under 4%, so the cost is implementation complexity and, for serving gains, dependence on a prototype extension of Punica's SGMV kernel; storage savings apply at inference and adapter-serving time only. The advantage is not uniform: on LLaMA-2 it loses to LoftQ at 7B and QLoRA at 70B, binarization with STE can be sensitive to scale and threshold initialization, and results rest on a single paper whose deployment kernel is a research prototype without production hardening.

Binary adapters reduce adapter storage by 13-16x versus FP16 LoRA; a research SGMV prototype holds 15.6x more adapters in HBM on one A100-80GB, and on Qwen2.5 benchmark averages exceed QLoRA by 0.8-3.5 points at every scale.
